speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what is the current state of the retail electricity market; (b) what are the reasons why iSwitch Energy decided to exit the energy retail business; (c) what will be the impact to consumers and businesses; and (d) how can electricity be kept affordable for households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry whether any steps will be taken to prevent or make it more difficult for electricity retailers to avoid their obligations to customers by withdrawing when the energy markets move against them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) whether electricity retailers are required to report their financial status regularly; (b) whether the Ministry monitors their financial health to ensure operational viability; (c) whether there will be a review on the number of energy retail licences needed to sustain the open electricity market; and (d) what are the plans when Singapore’s long-term piped gas contracts with Indonesia start expiring beyond 2023.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry with the recent rise in electricity prices and the exit of two electricity retailers (a) whether there will be support for consumers especially lower-income households given the increase in reliance on digital and work-from-home arrangements; and (b) what measures are in place to ensure that Singapore’s power supply remain stable and reliable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what are the causes of the sharp fluctuation in the spot prices of electricity since July 2021; and (b) based on the experience since inception of the Open Electricity Market (OEM) to date, what is the Ministry's assessment of the continued viability of the OEM for households.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry regarding the exit of some suppliers from the retail electricity market (a) what assistance will be provided to affected households and companies which will face unexpectedly higher tariff rates; and (b) whether the SP Group can honour the rates for which affected customers had contracted with the electricity retailers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what is the Government’s assessment of the vulnerability of the current model of electricity retailing; and (b) what measures can the Government take to help moderate the impact of higher energy prices on residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry in view of the discontinuation of electricity retailers from the open electricity market (a) whether the Ministry will review the requirements for licensing electricity retailers, such as assessing their paid-up capital, financial means, risk management and compliance measures; (b) what is the recourse for consumers and whether retailers are legally obliged to compensate consumers for early termination; and (c) whether the Ministry will consider licensing financial institutions as electricity retailers as they have the resources and are under strong governance and supervision by the authorities.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry given the recent withdrawal of electricity retailers (a) whether the future business model of electricity retailers will be reviewed to ensure that they are sustainable; (b) whether the Ministry will consider different selection criteria for new electricity retailers; and (c) whether the Ministry will assist families who may be impacted by the increase in electricity prices when helping them transit to more energy efficient appliances.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) with the rising cost of energy worldwide, what are the measures taken to secure the country’s access to energy; and (b) what are the measures taken to ensure that energy remains affordable to businesses and households in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) amid the current global fuel supply crunch and price volatility, what are its near- and longer-term implications on our energy security and affordability; (b) what are the measures and contingency plans in place to ensure energy supply reliability and resilience; and (c) whether current generating capacity can meet the electricity demand in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) how many electricity retailers are currently left in the market; (b) what measures will the Ministry put in place to ensure that there is a viable business left for the remaining retailers and the market remains competitive; and (c) whether there will be assistance provided to affected household and companies who may now face higher tariff rates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The shocks have been most intensely manifested in the market for natural gas, which is a fallback fuel for electricity generation in many, many countries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many major economies across Europe and Asia have low inventory levels and are moving quickly to secure sufficient fuel supplies for the winter.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These have compounded the impact on prices of fuel and electricity around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have received 28 PQs on energy-related matters.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore relies on imported natural gas for almost all our electricity production and is therefore highly exposed to global supply and demand shocks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Over the years, we have put in place measures to secure Singapore’s access to fuel supplies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since 1999, we have had long-term supply contracts for Piped Natural Gas (PNG) from Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Negotiations to renew some of these contracts are ongoing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is likely to last until the end of 2021 as the facility undergoes repair and upgrading.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Gas pressure of the supply from South Sumatra has also been affected due to higher demand from gas users upstream.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Energy Market Authority (EMA) is working with the gas importers to stabilise the PNG supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In 2013, we supplemented PNG with Liquified Natural Gas (LNG) by building an LNG terminal.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This allows us to tap gas sources further afield and is part and parcel of our diversification strategy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The LNG terminal has sufficient capacity to meet all of Singapore’s gas needs should PNG be unavailable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Earlier this year, EMA also appointed two new term LNG importers, bringing the total number of term LNG importers in Singapore to four.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, EMA ensures that there is sufficient generation capacity to convert the fuel to electricity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Taking into account planned and unplanned outages, we need to maintain spare generation capacity or reserve margin of at least 27% above peak electricity demand.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, the reserve margin stands at 52% – still significantly above 27%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Over the last 10 years, the excess capacity had been higher, mainly due to over-investment by private gencos in the early 2010s.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Going forward, we cannot always assume that the private sector will put in sufficient investments to build new generation capacity, even as the margin narrows over time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will touch on how we intend to address this though the Energy (Resilience Measures and Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In short, we have sufficient fuel supplies and generation capacity today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, given the unprecedented scale of this energy crunch, we are leaving nothing to chance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA has been working closely with industry stakeholders on pre-emptive measures to further secure Singapore’s fuel and electricity supply and ensure energy resilience and reliability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, we have established standby fuel facilities which gencos can draw upon if needed to generate electricity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, to complement the standby fuel facilities, EMA has informed gencos to contract sufficient fuel to at least meet their customers’ demands.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, in the extreme event that gencos are not willing to draw on gas reserves to generate electricity – perhaps due to risk aversion – EMA will engage the gencos directly to generate electricity using fuel from the standby facilities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Details of these measures are in EMA’s press release on 19 October 2021.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, these pre-emptive measures are extraordinary, but they are also necessary to secure our fuel and electricity supply during this extraordinary period.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have announced that we will quadruple our solar deployment by 2030, to generate at least two gigawatt-peak (GWp) of electricity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also announced last week that we will be importing up to four gigawatt (GW) of low-carbon electricity by 2035.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While this was primarily a move to decarbonise the power system, it will also reduce our reliance on natural gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond this, we will continue to explore other low-carbon alternatives like hydrogen and geothermal energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Collectively, these measures will make our power system more resilient and less susceptible to price and supply risks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will now touch on the electricity retailers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since the 2000s, EMA had progressively liberalised the electricity retail market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Electricity retailers buy electricity through the wholesale electricity market (WEM) to sell to consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They were generally able to offer prices which were priced lower than the regulated tariff in the last few years, because wholesale electricity prices were depressed below the long run marginal costs due to overcapacity in generation, and oversupply of gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Electricity Futures Market (EFM), set up in April 2015, also enabled retailers to hedge their price risks through electricity futures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Retailers can also offlay their risk to gencos through financial hedges such as Contracts for Differences (CfDs).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These have worked well in a stable market environment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the nationwide launch of the Open Electricity Market (OEM) in 2018, household consumers were able to benefit from greater choice, competitive pricing and innovative offers with no change to the reliability of their electricity supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, market conditions today are significantly more volatile than in 2018.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some market participants had not anticipated this and were not sufficiently prepared.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members are understandably concerned about why retailers are exiting the market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, several retailers were under-hedged when the global energy shocks and disruptions to our PNG supply caused wholesale electricity prices to spike.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These retailers now find themselves having to buy the unhedged portion of electricity at the high wholesale electricity prices and sell them at much lower contracted rates to consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, liquidity in the electricity futures market has also been affected.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Given the huge volatility, market makers were not prepared to take on significant positions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is similar to the situation in other commodity markets.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As a result, some electricity retailers are no longer able to sustain their operations in this challenging environment and thus, have chosen to exit the market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The unusually high number of exits reflects the severity of the global energy shock.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have observed the same phenomenon in other countries, such as the UK as well as Spain.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The key is to have a fair and robust system to ensure a smooth transition for customers affected by exiting retailers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Retailers who wish to exit the retail electricity market are required to first approach other retailers to take on those consumers at the same terms and conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Failing which, the consumer will be transferred to SP Group.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Consumers who are transferred to the SP Group can choose to purchase electricity from another retailer.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Security deposits from household consumers are safeguarded and will be refunded after offsetting outstanding charges.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Retailers are not allowed to charge customers an early termination fee.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will be no disruption to electricity supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will direct consumers who wish to seek compensation or file claims under their supply contracts with the retailers to the available channels.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Given the current challenging circumstances, EMA is open to allowing retailers facing challenges to suspend their operations by transferring their customers to SP Group while they strengthen their business.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In exchange, these retailers commit to provide an ex gratia payment to ease their customers' transition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Best Electric, Ohm Energy and UGS Energy have joined this arrangement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA is working closely with the remaining nine retailers who are still operating in the Open Electricity Market (OEM).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA is facilitating their efforts to hedge against future price volatility.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These include facilitating the sale of electricity futures contracts between retailers that are exiting the retail market to those that are staying.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA is also working closely with SGX to incentivise more market makers to participate in the electricity futures market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some Members of Parliament have asked if SP can continue to honour the prices and terms of the existing contracts that affected customers had contracted with their electricity retailers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The transferred households will need to pay the same regulated tariffs as all the other households and small businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This reflects the price SP pays to the gencos for the electricity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thus, for the transferred customers to pay less, the other consumers with SP will have to pay more than the regulated tariffs to cross-subsidise them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: A few Members have asked what the recent exit of retailers portend for the OEM.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Notwithstanding the recent exits, the OEM has benefited and continues to benefit many Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Since it was launched in November 2018, consumers have been able to enjoy increased choice and flexibility when buying electricity, ranging from fixed-price plans, discount-off-tariff (DOT) plans, or even wholesale electricity price plans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: More importantly, consumers who switch to retail price plans have been able to enjoy savings of up to 30% off the regulated tariff.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are currently nine remaining retailers in the OEM.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Depending on the severity and the duration of this energy crunch, more retailers may either exit or they may re-enter the market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members have asked whether EMA will be reviewing the number of electricity retail licensees needed to sustain the OEM.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is sufficient competition in the OEM today and EMA is committed to ensuring this.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Last but not least, the foundations of the OEM will need to be strengthened.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, OEM retailers are vetted and have to satisfy a stringent set of requirements before they are licensed to serve OEM consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is the current crisis that we are facing today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members have raised useful suggestions on how we can further strengthen these requirements and the futures market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I wanted to thank the Members for giving us more suggestions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore imports our energy needs and cannot be fully insulated from developments in the global energy market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Most consumers in Singapore have been cushioned somewhat so far.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These have risen by far less than the price of gas or wholesale electricity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, the sustained high fuel prices will eventually feed into our electricity bills to reflect the cost of electricity production.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many Members of this House have asked what the Government will be doing to help affected households and businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MTI will also work with MOF to monitor the situation and study whether further assistance is required for affected households and businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we are also conducting programmes to raise awareness of electricity conservation and facilitate efforts by households and businesses to reduce their utility bills.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, SP Services has been progressively replacing households’ analogue electricity meters with advanced electricity meters which allow them to track their energy consumption through the SP Utilities mobile app.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will help households better understand their electricity usage patterns and encourage them to be more energy efficient.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: NEA has also launched other energy saving initiatives such as the Climate Friendly Households Programme to encourage households to switch to more resource-efficient appliances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Eligible households are given vouchers to offset the costs of these appliances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We urge all consumers to use energy prudently and adopt energy conservation as a way of life.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Amongst major cities, our electricity supply is one of the most reliable and price competitive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our market is now being tested by an unprecedented storm in the global energy market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our commitment to this House is this: we will secure our energy supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will help vulnerable consumers weather the storm.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we will continue to make our energy sector even better.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: First of all, I want to thank the Minister for his reassuring reply on how we are going to deal with the ongoing energy crunch and volatility.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My question is going to be on the electricity retailers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the light of the current disruptions, as the Minister said, some retailers are ill-prepared for this current volatility, would the Government still recommend consumers to switch to the retail price plan?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second question is, while the OEM has indeed brought significant savings to households in the last few years – having discounts over the regulated rates and so on – does the Government see the need to review this, review the regime, given the situation that we are facing now, perhaps to have fewer, but stronger and more regulated retailers?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Or just having one, Singapore Power, but offering different price plans so that they can benefit from the scale efficiency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The OEM provides choices to consumers, notwithstanding the recent volatility, electricity retailers continue to offer competitively-priced retail price plans to interested consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Affected consumers who have switched back to the regulated tariffs, actually still have the option of choosing from other retailers that are able to suit their needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we encourage all consumers to study carefully, deliberate over which electricity price plan would best suit their needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the viability on the OEM, in my main reply, I think it still remains but we will need to continue to explore ways and means to strengthen the foundations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My Ministry will study how we can further strengthen the safeguards for the OEM, so as to better protect our consumers' interests.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If I can request Members to keep their questions short and no more than two supplementary questions, please.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I have one question: if the supply crunch continues to worsen over the next few months, in the longer term, then, what is MTI's strategy to reduce the national consumption, the demand, especially from industries, the sectorial angle.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think we have been constantly engaging the industry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Earlier and through the past year, I have mentioned that underlying the four switches of what we have been preparing for, underlying it is energy conservation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also want to encourage industry to consider using energy in a more efficient manner, because obviously there are peak demands and there are off-peak demands.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we hope that the industry will work closely with all of us in making sure that we can space out the peak demand versus the trough.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In terms of how we procure the gas prices, we are also looking at means of exploring other longer-term measures: importing low-carbon electricity, importing from the regional grid are some of these strategies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also exploring, as a much longer-term strategy, to reduce our reliance on importation and that would be to look at our solar power generation capacity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we are also looking at working with academia, the different institutions, as well as industry leaders in how we can access low-carbon hydrogen, carbon capture utilisation and storage as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we have a combination of all these measures to reduce our reliance on any one particular supply of energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On top of that, we are also exploring the use of energy storage systems in the form of batteries to see how we can provide a more stable power supply to reduce the intermittence from solar energy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have a related supplementary question for the Minister in terms of energy stability as well as security.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Today, 95% of Singapore's electricity still comes from natural gas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Minister talked about the pre-emptive measures of stockpiling as well as enabling the standby fuel facilities for gencos to be able to use this capacity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But from the high prices that we have seen for natural gas, how sustainable is this measure?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know that it sounds like supply is sufficient, but how sustainable is this, given the consumption and the heavy reliance on electricity?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At the same time, my second supplementary question is on the status of the genco supply and generation capacity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Does EMA monitor this and what is the current status of this capacity as well as that supply?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Generation companies should utilise their own fuel supply to meet electricity demand and only tap on the standby fuel facilities when needed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Minister has noted that the regulatory requirements for our Open Electricity Market (OEM) are probably inadequate to withstand a severe stress situation such as the current one.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: He identified four key things that are culminating to a perfect storm.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, how will the Government address the vulnerability of the current regulatory framework for the long-term sustainability of the OEM?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I guess this was designed and I guess we did not expect this perfect storm.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, specifically, what is the time frame you will be rolling out a new enhanced framework; anything on the hedging strategy, anything about the financial strength of the OEM?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The second question is whether the Government will consider, in the meantime, special support to the remaining electricity retailers for their continued operations and also most importantly, their commitments to the consumers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, how are those who are still surviving, including SP, going to manage the influx of the new customers, which it will now have to serve?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Indeed, there is a cost to regulation and this cost ultimately would be borne by consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the requirements are too onerous, then fewer retailers may be willing to participate in the market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Therefore, if there are fewer retailers, there will be less choice and there will be less competitive plans for consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, retailers and their shareholders know that if they should exit without regard for their customers' interests, they may not be granted retail licences henceforth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thus, over the last decade, up to 2020, only five other retailers have left the market and many of them cited the intense market competition as the main reason for their exit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This demonstrates that our safeguards in the past would have probably sufficed not just in our market, but in most market conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This episode, this unprecedented crisis, has highlighted some learning points for us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, we have to be also practical and realistic when instituting safeguards because it would be neither feasible nor economically prudent for us to institute safeguards that can cover every potential possible eventuality.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Doing so would lead to significant costs for consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the measures that SP is taking to manage the influx of new consumers which it must now serve, the objective of shifting consumers back to SP is to ensure that there is no break in electricity provision.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SP has put in place measures to make the transition for affected customers and consumers as seamless as possible.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This transition back to SP is fully automated and the affected consumers do not have to take any action.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: SP will also follow up with consumers, post the transition, with an email or letter notification, informing them of the transfer.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Affected consumers who wish to remain with SP, do not need to take any further action.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Consumers are also free to switch out to other retailers thereafter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have one supplementary question for the Minister concerning whether he has any interim data to share on the customers who have been affected by the exit of the independent retailers?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What I mean is, since the exit of iSwitch and others, their customers would have to make certain decisions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From those announcements till now, can Minister share whether most customers who are displaced have decided to stay with SP for time being or have they switched to the larger retailers who are also generators called gen-tailers?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Or have they actually taken the plunge to go with another independent retailer?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the short answer is that I do not have the data because it happened quite recently.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I think we will monitor her question as posed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, we have every intention to do so.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And perhaps at the subsequent Sitting, if she can file another PQ, we would be quite happy to update her.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hear from the previous answer to the hon Sylvia Lim that you do not have the current numbers on how many would possibly be able to novate.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But a follow-up question is, how would the regulator EMA, in this case, ensure that the code is adhered to by those retailers who are exiting the market, so that these negotiations do carry on and benefit the end consumer.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The next is related to the ex gratia payment that Minister had mentioned and which was also in the EMA press release.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How would the retailers be getting in touch with their customers, in terms of possible ex gratia payment to ease the transition?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In part of my earlier reply, I said the retailers will work with EMA and they will, of course, work with other retailers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And as a last resort where SP comes in to take over that, in the form of a regulated tariff, there is a sequence and a mechanism to it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Suffice to say, today, that what EMA will do is that they will continually work with existing retailers to ensure that the transfer is seamless and to also ensure that there is a fair code of practice being adhered to.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thus far, the novation has happened fairly seamlessly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are existing retailers that are still in the business and I think that everyone is watching the situation quite carefully as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think the stability that we have provided is that very pre-emptive move to make sure that the supplies have been fortified.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have made sure that the supply of gas for the generation of electricity is actually ensured, so that our reliability and our resilience is preserved.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We probably would have more points put in there to ensure that our resilience continues to be reinforced.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This applies even to the retailers that have already exited.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This round, the crisis was unprecedented and there are significant challenges to retailers because they were not sufficiently hedged.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While they may have some existing hedges which can be unwound,  some of the retailers have suffered significant losses this round over the last few months.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because, the hedging is, I think we require them to maintain 50% hedge, so, because they were not fully hedged, therefore, that swing, the huge volatility swing has resulted in them suffering significant losses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ostensibly, we cannot possibly predict and pre-empt every single episode as I have shared earlier on in my answer to Ms Foo's PQ.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we covered every single instance of volatility, up to the different standard deviations, it would be very, very costly for us and not tenable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But we will make use of this opportunity to learn from it and also study how we can further strengthen and tighten it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that gives the Member the reassurance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How much leverage does EMA have over foreign gas suppliers to ensure that disruptions and low pressure do not become a regular occurrence, for example, through the imposition of liquidated damages?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And have these levers being exercised so far?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: About 79% of 1-room to 2-room households versus just 40% of landed property households.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is from data from a PQ I asked in January.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This means that the lower-income group has been paying elevated regulated tariff prices for several months already.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government consider a special one-off additional electricity rebate to assist these lower-income households during this difficult period?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have shared also in my earlier statements, either during Committee of Supply 2021 or in some of my earlier Parliamentary speeches that,  the 4-room HDB flats and for the 3-room HDB flats, the rebates amount to about six months of rebates per year, and I think for some, four months per year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, the low-income households are the ones that we are also very, very concerned about.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am not at liberty at this particular point in time to release further details, because obviously, we are still working out the details with MOF.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, to summarise, the low-income households get a higher proportion of the U-Save vouchers compared to other types of households.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In terms of other negotiations, as to how we talk to other suppliers and so on, I think because it compromises our energy security and it also compromises our negotiation powers, at this particular point in time, I am not at liberty to share them and I hope you understand.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, the Minister mentioned just now about trying to enhance consumers' reduction of their energy consumption to manage their costs while also allowing us to achieve our climate goals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What more can the Ministry do to enhance this even further, in terms of letting consumers manage their costs through reduced energy consumption?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second question is related to what Member Mr Gerald Giam asked.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am very concerned about the affordability of electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Consumers can no longer enjoy the very competitive prices under OEM, compared to the regulated tariffs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, the question is, in the worst-case scenario of retailers falling to zero – we do not want that to happen, but if it falls to zero from nine currently – do we have to go to U-Save rebates for vulnerable families going forward many times, given the volatility of the markets?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And if it is triggered, what more can we do to other groups, rather than just the vulnerable groups?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there certain segments that we can help, beyond the vulnerable segments, to weather the storm?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For a period of time, the electricity retailers were generally able to offer prices lower than the regulated tariff because the wholesale electricity prices were depressed below cost due to the over capacity in generation and oversupply of gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I think I did intimate to Members of the House, in fact, I gave a very strong point earlier this year that that low prices are not sustainable and that it will go.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Even if we do go into low-carbon electricity, we will still have to import, because geographically, we are naturally disadvantaged.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we still have to import the rest of it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I think the Member's point about how do we — I mean, the way I have underscored it is really about energy conservation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The OEM is not just simply about offering our consumers discount off regulated tariffs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: More pertinently, it offers a variety of fixed price plans and variable price plans to our consumers so that they can select the plan that best suits their needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, the only sustainable way looking forward and one of those things that I have been preaching constantly is that we would strongly encourage all Singaporeans to adopt energy conservation as our way of life.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We can turn the lights off when we are not in the room.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We can opt to use the fan more often rather than using air-conditioning.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We can, in air-conditioning rooms, push the temperature up by a few degrees, we do not have to bring it down so low and wear a sweater.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And switching to more energy-efficient appliances where possible.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I think that NEA has worked very well with us to put the ticks for appliances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The more ticks, the more efficient the appliances in terms of conservation of energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that with every single bit, we can all come together and help.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also committed to a low carbon footprint moving forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think you have read in the news today about what is happening in Glasgow and UN Climate Change Conference (COP26) and how this global warming is going to create catastrophic disastrous consequences for us if we do not lower our carbon emission.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that with that collective effort, we can all come together and make this a greener and a lower energy-requiring environment to live in.
